text: Built-in tests catch structural problems — a null, a duplicate. They can't catch a value that's structurally fine but wrong, like a payment amount that somehow comes out negative. This lesson writes a custom test for exactly that.

A generic test's query returns the rows that fail the check. This one selects any row where the given column is less than zero — model and column name are parameters, not hardcoded, which is what makes the test reusable.
Once defined under tests slash generic, non_negative gets applied in yml exactly the same way as unique or not_null, on orders dot amount, alongside the built-in tests already protecting order_id.
Running dbt test against orders checks this automatically. If any row ever has a negative amount, the test fails and names exactly which model and column — no one has to remember to check by hand.

A comment saying a rule exists relies on every future developer reading it. A test runs on every single build, enforced, not just remembered. Next: generating real documentation and the lineage graph from this same project.
